title: KV + Scheduler microprobe: field notes and regression ledger
body:
Context and intent:
This is a lightweight, informal ledger capturing a week-long run of microprobe experiments that combine KV-cache semantics with scheduler policy changes. Goal: identify recurring p99 regressions caused by interactions between KV cache eviction behavior and the new queue-aware scheduler heuristics. This doc purposely keeps raw observations, failure modes, and reproducible commands together so on-call and perf can iterate fast.

High-level summary (one-paragraph):
- We observed two distinct tail modes across samples: (A) cache-miss amplification where a long-tail originating from synchronous KV prefetching under high concurrency pushes p99 up by 15-40% and (B) scheduler-induced head-of-line blocking when large long-context requests monopolize the batch window, raising end-to-end p95/p99 for small requests. Hypothesis: the current scheduler favors throughput at cost of isolation; combined with eager KV prefetch it creates bursts of device memory pressure and PCIe flushing.

Experiment harness and reproducibility notes:
- Microprobe harness: `microprobe-v0.9` (local branch: `probe/queue-prefetch`) - lightweight runner that replays traces and synthetic injectors against the runtime binary.
- Command used (container): `./microprobe --trace traces/short-long-mix.json --spawn 48 --batch-window-ms 12 --kv-mode eager --sched-policy queue-aware --kernel-registry kernels/fast.json --out perf/kv-queue-20241107.csv`
- Key knobs we toggled:
  - kv-mode: [eager, lazy, lazy-prefetch, prewarm-only]
  - sched-policy: [fifo, strict-priority, queue-aware, deadline-aware]
  - batch-window-ms: [6, 12, 25, 50]
  - concurrency: [8, 16, 32, 48]
  - kernel-registry: [fast (fused-gemm+flash), compatibility (triton-default), quant-8bit-optimized]

Workload composition (short description):
- Mixed client mix with heavy skew: 80% short (<=64 tokens) low-kv footprint requests, 15% medium (128-512 tokens) occasional KV hits, 5% long (>=2048 tokens) high KV pressure. We interleave TTL-expiry events to simulate eviction storms. Traces are synthetic but seeded from production trace histogram (trace id `seed-20241011`).

Observed metrics (selected):
- Typical baseline (fifo, kv-mode lazy, batch-window 12ms, concurrency 16): p50 8ms, p95 34ms, p99 82ms, GPU SM util 32%, avg kernel latency 4.1ms per token.
- Regressed scenario (queue-aware, kv-mode eager, concurrency 48, batch-window 25ms): p50 9ms (+12%), p95 46ms (+35%), p99 112ms (+36%), GPU SM util 68% but with 3x variance spikes; PCIe stall events detectable in perf counters.

Trace slices and root-cause clues:
- Slice A (KV miss amplification):
  - Pattern: medium request triggers a prefetch that wins the scheduling lottery; many concurrent prefetches allocate new KV segments causing transient device OOM-ish behavior; runtime falls back to host copy and serialized transfers.
  - Evidence: increased memcpy H2D time, `kv-prefetch` logs show multiple parallel segment allocations; smoothed KV hit-rate drops from 0.89 -> 0.62 for short requests immediately following the wave.

- Slice B (HoL blocking from long contexts):
  - Pattern: new queue-aware policy groups by estimated token work; long-context job lands in an earlier slot and forces batch window extension to hit predicted throughput targets; short requests then await the extended window.
  - Evidence: scheduler traces show `window_adjust` events; batch sizes balloon from 6->20 while short requests were present; p95 for short requests increases by factor 2.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Eager KV prefetch combined with high concurrency creates allocation storms that serialize on PCIe and cudaMalloc fallback paths, causing tail amplification.
2) Queue-aware policy's grouping heuristic (group-by-estimated-tokens descending) lacks strict latency isolation for small requests.
3) Kernel selection amplifies the issue: the `fast` registry picks fused kernels that have worse memory locality under mixed batch shapes, increasing memory pressure.

Short-term mitigations tested (results):
- Switch kv-mode -> lazy-prefetch (only prefetch when request is scheduled to a GPU within X ms): reduced p99 by ~18% in high-concurrency tests.
- Enforce per-request latency buckets (soft isolation): limit batch-window expansion for buckets marked latency-sensitive; p95 improves but throughput drops ~6%.
- Limit concurrent prefetches per-device to N=8: reduces allocation spikes, p99 improved ~22% at cost of slightly higher p50 for long requests.

Reproducible tiny testcases to iterate locally:
- script: `testcases/kv-spike.sh` (pseudo):
  1) start runtime with `--kv-mode eager --prefetch-limit 0 --sched queue-aware`
  2) spawn 40 short clients + 8 long clients with TTL churn
  3) capture `nvprof` counters around memcpy and cudaMalloc fallback
  4) compare with run where `--prefetch-limit 8`

Regression ledger (commits and quick notes):
- commit 3f7a2b7 (probe/queue-prefetch): initial harness with queue-aware instrumentation. Observed stable baseline.
- commit a8d9c01 (runtime/sched): changed grouping heuristic to sort by tokens desc -> introduced HoL blocking (p95 spike).
- commit b3e6f4a (kv): added eager prefetch path; coincides with allocation storms in stress runs.
- commit f9d02c2 (kernels): introduced `fast` fused kernels; increased SM util but worsened tail under mixed shapes.

Open questions / unresolved angles:
- Is the real fix algorithmic (scheduler redesign) or pragmatic (rate-limit prefetch + small request isolation)?
- Can we implement an adaptive prefetch limiter that responds to device fragmentation signals (cudaMalloc latency, OOM events)?
- Do fused kernels need a different memory allocation strategy (pre-reserve KV slab) when mixed batch shapes are detected?

Action items / next steps (owners and targets):
- [Diego] prototype adaptive prefetch limiter (PR draft) — target: 2024-11-20.
- [Maya] add finer-grained sched tracing (per-batch tokens, per-request priority markers) to help disambiguate HoL in traces — target: 2024-11-15.
- [Ethan] run nightly microprobe suite with `--prefetch-limit` sweep and post results to perf dashboard — target: ongoing, include in weekly perf digest.
- [Aisha] synthesize a lightweight load-shedding policy for short-request buckets to enforce soft SLOs — POC by 2024-11-28.

Notes for on-call and SRE:
- If p99 climbs in production coinciding with a new runtime deploy where `kv-mode` or `sched` changed, roll back `kv-mode` to `lazy-prefetch` and reduce concurrency via target limits on dedicated pools.
- Useful quick checks: `kubectl logs runtime --grep kv-prefetch`, GPU memcpy counters, and the `scheduler_windows` trace table in tracing UI.

Appendix: small paste of an example perf CSV (headers simplified):
- run_id,commit,kv_mode,sched,batch_ms,conc,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,sm_util
- r-20241107-1,3f7a2b7,lazy,fifo,12,16,8,34,82,32%
- r-20241107-2,f9d02c2,eager,queue-aware,25,48,9,46,112,68%
- r-20241109-3,f9d02c2,lazy-prefetch,queue-aware,25,48,8,38,92,54%

Free-form notes (brainstorm / half-baked ideas):
- Consider an explicit small-request fast-path that disables prefetch and forces a tiny preallocated KV slab per-request. Could be a good trade off for web-tier latencies.
- Explore kernel registry hints: annotated kernels with `memory-friendliness` score; scheduler consults that when forming batches to avoid mixing high-memory kernels with variable-length batches.
- Would love an eviction backpressure signal surfaced from KV manager to scheduler so prefetches can be slowed when fragmentation gets high.

End of doc. Keep this as a living ledger — update with new commit rows and any follow-up perf runs.
